craft.name: Apollo Lunar Module
craft.subtitle: The lander that carried astronauts to the Moon's surface

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Apollo crewed Moon landings

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1969 (Apollo 11, first landing)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired (last flew 1972)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 7.04 m tall, 9.4 m across the landing legs

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 15,103 kg (Apollo 11 LM, fueled)

facts.label: About
facts.value: The Lunar Module was a two-part spacecraft built only to fly in space and land on the Moon. Two astronauts rode it down to the surface while a third stayed in orbit. When it was time to leave, the top half blasted off and used the bottom half as its launch pad.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It never needed to be streamlined, because it never flew through air. That is why it looks so boxy and spidery.

craft.name: Cassini-Huygens
craft.subtitle: Orbited Saturn for 13 years and dropped a probe on Titan

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Saturn orbiter and Titan probe

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, ESA, and the Italian Space Agency (ASI)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Mission ended 2017 (dove into Saturn on purpose)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 6.7 m high, 4 m wide

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 5,712 kg at launch (with fuel and the Huygens probe)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Cassini spent 13 years orbiting Saturn, studying its rings, its storms, and its moons. It carried Europe's Huygens probe, which parachuted to the surface of Titan in 2005. At the end, Cassini was steered into Saturn so it could never crash into and contaminate a moon that might host life.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Cassini found evidence of a global ocean of liquid water under the icy crust of Saturn's moon Enceladus.

craft.name: Chandra X-ray Observatory
craft.subtitle: A space telescope that sees the universe in X-rays

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: X-ray space telescope

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (operated by the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1999 (Space Shuttle Columbia)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 13.8 m long, 19.5 m across the solar arrays

facts.label: About
facts.value: Chandra studies the hottest, most violent places in the universe, like exploding stars and matter falling into black holes. X-rays cannot get through Earth's air, so an X-ray telescope has to work in space. Its mirrors are shaped like nested barrels so X-rays skim off them at shallow angles.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Chandra's mirrors are among the smoothest ever made.

craft.subtitle: A car-sized science lab exploring Gale Crater on Mars

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mars Science Laboratory

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3 m long, 2.7 m wide, 2.2 m tall

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: Curiosity is a nuclear-powered rover about the size of a small car. It drills into rocks and analyzes them in onboard labs to learn whether Mars once had conditions that could support microbes. It found that Gale Crater once held a lake of fresh water.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Curiosity was lowered to the ground on cables by a hovering rocket stage called the sky crane.

craft.name: Dawn
craft.subtitle: The first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Asteroid belt orbiter (Vesta and Ceres)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Mission ended 2018 (out of fuel, still orbiting Ceres)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 19.7 m across the solar arrays

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 1,217.7 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Dawn explored the two biggest objects in the asteroid belt, Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres. It used ion engines that push gently but for a very long time, which let it leave orbit around one world and travel to another. At Ceres it found bright salt deposits left by briny water.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Dawn's ion engines pushed with about the force of a sheet of paper resting on your hand.

craft.name: Galileo
craft.subtitle: The first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Jupiter orbiter and atmospheric probe

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL (with partners in Germany and other countries)

facts.label: Launch

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Mission ended 2003 (sent into Jupiter on purpose)

facts.label: Real size

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Galileo's big umbrella-like antenna never fully opened, so engineers rewrote its software to send data through a much smaller antenna.

craft.name: Hubble Space Telescope
craft.subtitle: The school-bus-sized telescope orbiting Earth since 1990

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Visible and ultraviolet space telescope

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and ESA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1990 (Space Shuttle Discovery)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 13.2 m long, 4.2 m wide

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 12,200 kg (after the last servicing mission in 2009)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Hubble orbits above the blurring effect of Earth's air, so it takes extremely sharp pictures of planets, nebulas, and galaxies. Astronauts visited it five times to repair and upgrade it. Its measurements helped show that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Hubble has no rocket thrusters. It turns by spinning heavy wheels inside, using Newton's third law.

craft.name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
craft.subtitle: The first aircraft to fly on another planet

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mars technology demonstration (rode with Perseverance)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 2020 (first flight April 19, 2021)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Flights ended January 2024 (rotor damage)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 0.49 m tall, rotors 1.2 m tip to tip

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: Ingenuity was a small solar-powered helicopter that proved powered flight is possible on Mars, where the air is about 1% as thick as Earth's. It was planned for five test flights and ended up making 72. It also scouted the terrain ahead of the Perseverance rover.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its rotor blades spun at about 2,400 revolutions per minute to get enough lift in Mars's thin air.

craft.name: James Webb Space Telescope
craft.subtitle: The largest space telescope ever launched
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: James Webb Space Telescope (A)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Infrared space telescope

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, ESA, and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 2021 (Ariane 5)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: sunshield 21.2 m x 14.2 m (about a tennis court)

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 6,200 kg

facts.label: About
facts.value: Webb sees infrared light, which lets it look through dust clouds and back to some of the first galaxies that formed after the Big Bang. Its gold-coated mirror is 6.5 m across, made of 18 hexagonal segments. A five-layer sunshield keeps the telescope colder than minus 220 degrees Celsius so its own heat does not swamp the faint signals.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Webb had to unfold itself in space, like origami, because it was too big to fit inside any rocket.

craft.name: Juno
craft.subtitle: A solar-powered spacecraft orbiting Jupiter's poles

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Jupiter polar orbiter

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL (led by Southwest Research Institute)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 2011 (arrived 2016)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating in an extended mission (last confirmed mid-2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: body 3.5 m; more than 20 m across the solar arrays

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 3,625 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Juno loops over Jupiter's poles to study what is inside the giant planet, including its gravity, magnetic field, and deep atmosphere. It is the first solar-powered spacecraft sent that far from the Sun, so it needs enormous solar arrays. Its radiation vault shields its electronics from Jupiter's intense radiation.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: At Jupiter, Juno's huge solar arrays make only about 500 watts, enough for about five old-style 100-watt light bulbs. Near Earth, the same arrays would make about 14,000 watts.

craft.name: Kepler
craft.subtitle: The planet hunter that found thousands of worlds

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Exoplanet survey telescope

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired 2018 (out of fuel)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 4.7 m tall, 2.7 m wide

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 1,052.4 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Kepler stared at the same patch of sky for years, measuring the brightness of about 150,000 stars. When a planet passes in front of its star, the star dims very slightly, and Kepler watched for those dips. It showed that planets are common around other stars.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Kepler's camera was the largest NASA had ever flown in space at the time, with about 95 million pixels.

craft.name: Parker Solar Probe
craft.subtitle: The spacecraft that flies through the Sun's outer atmosphere

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Close-up study of the Sun's corona and solar wind

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (built by Johns Hopkins APL)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3 m tall; heat shield 2.3 m across

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 685 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Parker Solar Probe dives closer to the Sun than any spacecraft before it, passing through the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona. A thick carbon heat shield always faces the Sun, keeping the instruments behind it near room temperature. It studies how the solar wind gets its speed.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: At closest approach it moves at about 700,000 km/h, the fastest speed of any human-made object.

craft.name: Perseverance Rover
craft.subtitle: Collecting rock samples in Jezero Crater on Mars

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mars 2020: search for signs of ancient life

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026). Science is paused while engineers fix a radio problem.

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3 m long, 2.7 m wide, 2.2 m tall

facts.label: About
facts.value: Perseverance explores an ancient river delta in Jezero Crater, looking for signs that microbes once lived on Mars. It drills rock cores and seals them in tubes for a possible future mission to bring back to Earth. It also carried the Ingenuity helicopter.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Perseverance carries two microphones. In 2021 it made the first audio recording on Mars using a microphone, capturing a Martian breeze.

craft.name: TESS
craft.subtitle: Searching the nearest, brightest stars for new planets
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) (A)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (led by MIT)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 2018 (Falcon 9)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3.9 m across its solar panels

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 362 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: TESS uses four wide-angle cameras to watch most of the sky for tiny dips in starlight caused by orbiting planets. It focuses on bright, nearby stars, so other telescopes like Webb can follow up on the planets it finds. It took over the planet-hunting job from Kepler.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: TESS's orbit is timed with the Moon: it goes around Earth twice for every one lunar orbit.

craft.name: Viking Lander
craft.subtitle: The first US spacecraft to land and work on Mars

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Viking 1 and 2: Mars landers and orbiters

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Status

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3 m wide, 2 m tall

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: Two Viking landers touched down on Mars in 1976 and sent back the first color pictures from its surface. They scooped up soil and ran experiments to test for life. The results were puzzling, and scientists still discuss them today.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Viking Lander 1 kept working for more than six years on Mars.

craft.name: Voyager
craft.subtitle: Twin probes now travelling between the stars

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Grand tour of the outer planets, now interstellar

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1977 (Voyager 1 and 2)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Both are still in contact from interstellar space. Since Nov. 14, 2026, Voyager 1 has sent only a basic radio signal and no data while engineers work on a computer problem.

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: high-gain antenna 3.7 m across; magnetometer boom 13 m

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 722 kg each at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: The twin Voyagers flew past Jupiter and Saturn, and Voyager 2 went on to Uranus and Neptune, the only spacecraft ever to visit them. Both have now left the Sun's bubble of solar wind and are in interstellar space. Each carries a golden record with sounds and images from Earth.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: In November 2026 Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth, so its radio signals take a full day to arrive.

facts.value: The ISS circles Earth about every 90 minutes, about 400 km up. People have lived on board continuously since November 2000, running experiments on how space affects bodies, plants, and materials. It was built piece by piece over many years by five space agencies.

facts.value: The station and its crew are in free fall around Earth. That is why astronauts float, even though gravity there is still about 90% as strong as on the ground.

facts.value: NASA

facts.value: The Space Shuttle orbiter launched like a rocket and landed like a glider. It carried astronauts and large cargo, launched and repaired the Hubble Space Telescope, and helped build the ISS. Heat-resistant tiles on its belly protected it when it came back through the atmosphere.

craft.name: Gemini
craft.subtitle: The two-person capsule that practiced the moves for the Moon

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Project Gemini: 10 crewed flights in Earth orbit (1965 to 1966)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1965 (first crewed flight, Gemini 3)

facts.label: Status

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: About 5.7 m long and 3 m across the base.

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: Gemini carried two astronauts and was the bridge between Mercury and Apollo. Its crews practiced what a Moon trip would need: spacewalks, flights of up to two weeks, and meeting and docking with another spacecraft in orbit.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: In December 1965, Gemini 6A and Gemini 7 flew within about 30 cm (1 foot) of each other. It was the first time two crewed spacecraft met in orbit.

craft.name: Mercury Friendship 7
craft.subtitle: The capsule that carried John Glenn around Earth

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mercury-Atlas 6: first American crewed orbital flight

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: February 20, 1962

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired after one flight (now at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: About 2.7 m (9 ft) tall and 1.9 m wide at the bottom, small enough that Glenn barely fit inside.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 1,350 kg

facts.label: About
facts.value: John Glenn flew Friendship 7 around Earth three times in just under five hours. A warning signal suggested the heat shield might be loose, so he kept the retrorocket pack strapped on during reentry. The heat shield turned out to be fine.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: At each sunrise Glenn saw glowing specks drifting outside his window and called them fireflies. They turned out to be bits of frost from the capsule's small steering thrusters, which Scott Carpenter proved on the next flight by tapping the wall.

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Status

facts.value: NASA

craft.name: Magellan
craft.subtitle: Mapped Venus through its clouds with radar

facts.label: Mission

facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.value: Each rover was planned to work for about 90 Martian days. Spirit lasted more than six years and Opportunity almost 15. Both found rocks and minerals that formed in water, showing that early Mars was much wetter than today.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Opportunity drove 45.16 km (28.06 miles) on Mars. That was the record for driving on another world until Perseverance passed it in October 2026.

craft.name: Spitzer Space Telescope
craft.subtitle: Saw the universe in infrared, the light of heat

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Infrared space telescope, one of NASA's four Great Observatories

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL / Caltech

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: August 25, 2003

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired January 30, 2020

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: About 4 m (13 ft) tall.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 950 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Spitzer detected infrared light, which is heat, so it could see through dust clouds to find newborn stars and study planets around other stars. It had to stay very cold, so it trailed behind Earth in its own orbit around the Sun.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: In 2017 it helped reveal seven Earth-size planets around the star TRAPPIST-1.

craft.name: Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope
craft.subtitle: Watches the sky for the most energetic light in the universe
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Fermi Gamma-ray Large Area Space Telescope

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Gamma-ray observatory

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, U.S. Department of Energy, and partners in France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Sweden

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 2.9 m tall; solar panels 15 m tip to tip

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 4,303 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Gamma rays are the highest-energy form of light. Fermi scans the whole sky about every three hours, catching gamma-ray bursts, flaring black holes and spinning neutron stars called pulsars.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Fermi found two giant bubbles of gamma rays above and below the center of our Milky Way, each about 25,000 light-years tall.

craft.name: Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory
craft.subtitle: Raced to catch gamma-ray bursts, the biggest explosions in the universe

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Gamma-ray burst observatory

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, with partners in the UK and Italy

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: November 20, 2004

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Re-entered Earth's atmosphere November 4, 2026, after its orbit decayed

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 5.6 m tall; solar panels 4 m long

facts.label: About
facts.value: When Swift spotted a gamma-ray burst, it turned itself toward the burst in about a minute and a half, all on its own, to watch the fading afterglow in X-rays, ultraviolet and visible light. It also studied comets, exploding stars and black holes for almost 22 years.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was named after the swift, a small bird that can turn quickly in flight.

craft.name: Terra
craft.subtitle: The flagship of NASA's Earth-watching satellites

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Earth Observing System flagship: land, oceans, air and energy balance

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, with instruments from Japan and Canada

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: December 18, 1999

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Ending: science data stops December 1, 2026; power-off planned January 2027 (as of Nov 17, 2026)

facts.label: Real size

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 5,190 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Terra's instruments measure land, oceans, clouds, air pollution and Earth's energy balance at the same time. Designed for six years, it worked for 27, building a long record of wildfires, ice, forests and cities.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its MODIS camera images nearly the whole Earth every one to two days.

craft.name: Aqua
craft.subtitle: Tracks Earth's water: clouds, rain, ice and oceans

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Earth Observing System water-cycle mission

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, with instruments from Japan and Brazil

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Still working, but out of fuel for orbit boosts, so it is slowly drifting lower (as of November 2026).

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 4.8 m x 16.7 m x 8 m with its solar array out

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 2,934 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Aqua is named for water. It measures water vapor, clouds, rain, sea ice, snow and ocean temperatures, helping weather forecasters and climate scientists. It crosses the equator in the afternoon, so it sees places at a different time of day than Terra.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Aqua was designed to last six years and has been working for more than 24.

craft.name: Landsat 8
craft.subtitle: Part of the longest-running record of Earth's land from space

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Earth land-imaging satellite

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: February 11, 2013

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 2,780 kg (6,133 lb)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Landsat satellites have photographed Earth's land since 1972. Landsat 8 covers the whole planet every 16 days, so scientists can track crops, forests, glaciers, cities and wildfire scars over decades.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Each Landsat 8 scene covers a strip of ground about 185 km wide.

craft.name: SOHO
craft.subtitle: Has watched the Sun for three decades
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Solar and Heliospheric Observatory

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: ESA and NASA

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 4.3 m tall; 9.5 m across its solar panels

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 1,850 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: SOHO sits about 1.5 million km from Earth, at a spot where it can see the Sun all the time. It studies the Sun's interior, its outer atmosphere and the solar wind, and it gives early warning of solar storms.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Although it was built to study the Sun, SOHO is the greatest comet finder in history. It passed 5,000 comets in 2024, most of them spotted by volunteers looking at its images.

craft.name: Stardust
craft.subtitle: Caught comet dust and brought it home

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Comet Wild 2 sample return

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired March 24, 2011 (sample capsule landed January 15, 2006)

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 385 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Stardust flew through the dust around comet Wild 2 in 2004 and caught tiny particles. Its capsule parachuted into Utah in 2006, the first time material from a comet was brought back to Earth.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It caught the dust in aerogel, one of the lightest solids ever made, which slowed the speeding grains gently, like a very soft catcher's mitt.

craft.name: Deep Impact
craft.subtitle: Fired an impactor into a comet to see what's inside

facts.label: Mission

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: About
facts.value: On July 4, 2005, Deep Impact released a 372 kg impactor into the path of comet Tempel 1. The flyby spacecraft watched the crash, which blasted out a bright cloud of dust and ice and showed what the comet's surface was made of.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: The impactor hit the comet at about 10 km per second, or roughly 37,000 km/h.

craft.name: MESSENGER
craft.subtitle: The first spacecraft to orbit Mercury
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging (MESSENGER)

facts.value: NASA / Johns Hopkins APL

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Mission ended April 30, 2015 (crashed into Mercury as planned)

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 1,108 kg at launch, more than half of it fuel

facts.label: About
facts.value: MESSENGER used flybys of Earth, Venus and Mercury to slow down enough to enter orbit around Mercury in March 2011. It mapped the whole planet and found evidence of water ice in polar craters that never see sunlight.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: A heat-resistant sunshade kept the spacecraft near room temperature while its sunny side faced up to about 370 C (700 F).

craft.name: 2001 Mars Odyssey

facts.label: Mission

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Launch

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Odyssey has paused its science because one of the spinning wheels it uses to point itself stopped working. Engineers are testing it and hope to restart science in late November 2026.

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: Odyssey mapped the minerals of Mars and found large amounts of water ice just under the surface near the poles. For years it has also relayed messages between rovers on Mars and Earth.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It is named after the book and film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

craft.name: Solar Dynamics Observatory
craft.subtitle: Films the Sun in ultra-high definition
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Solar Dynamics Observatory (GitHub mirror)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 3,100 kg at launch, fueled

facts.label: About
facts.value: SDO photographs the whole Sun in several colors of light about every 10 seconds. It tracks sunspots, flares and the Sun's magnetic field to help scientists understand and predict space weather.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: SDO sends back about 1.5 terabytes of data every day.

craft.name: STEREO
craft.subtitle: Twin spacecraft that gave the first 3D views of solar storms
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Solar TErrestrial RElations Observatory (STEREO) (GitHub mirror)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (two spacecraft)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.value: STEREO-A operating (as of Nov 2026); STEREO-B lost contact in 2014

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 620 kg each

facts.label: About
facts.value: The two STEREO spacecraft spread out ahead of and behind Earth in its orbit around the Sun. Seeing from two angles, they made 3D views of eruptions on the Sun, and in 2011 they let scientists see the entire Sun at once for the first time.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: STEREO-A has gone all the way around the Sun and caught up with Earth again from behind, passing Earth in 2023.

craft.name: Deep Space 1

facts.label: About
facts.value: Deep Space 1 tested 12 new technologies, including an ion engine that used electricity to push out xenon gas. It then flew past asteroid Braille and comet Borrelly and took close-up pictures of the comet's core.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its ion engine ran for more than 16,000 hours, a record at the time.

craft.name: NEAR Shoemaker

facts.label: About
facts.value: NEAR orbited asteroid 433 Eros for a year and mapped its rocky, cratered surface. It was not built to land, but on February 12, 2001 the team set it down gently on Eros, and it kept sending data from the surface for about two more weeks.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was renamed in honor of Eugene Shoemaker, a planetary geologist famous for studying impact craters.

craft.name: LADEE

facts.value: The Moon has an extremely thin atmosphere called an exosphere. LADEE flew low over the Moon to sample it and to check whether dust floats above the surface. It also tested sending data by laser.

craft.name: Explorer 1

facts.value: Explorer 1 was a slim tube riding on top of the rocket's last stage. Its cosmic-ray instrument, built by James Van Allen's team, found belts of trapped radiation around Earth, now called the Van Allen belts.

craft.name: Compton Gamma Ray Observatory

facts.value: Compton carried four instruments that covered a huge range of gamma-ray energies. It found that gamma-ray bursts come from all directions in the sky, a clue that they happen in faraway galaxies rather than in our own.

facts.value: At about 16,300 kg, it was the heaviest astrophysics payload the Space Shuttle had carried up to that time.

craft.name: WMAP
craft.subtitle: Measured the age of the universe from the Big Bang's afterglow
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP)

facts.value: NASA

facts.value: WMAP mapped the cosmic microwave background, faint heat left over from the early universe, across the whole sky. Its measurements pinned the age of the universe at about 13.77 billion years and showed how much of it is normal matter, dark matter and dark energy.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It worked about 1.5 million km from Earth, on the side away from the Sun, where it could stay shaded and very cold.

craft.name: Aquarius / SAC-D

facts.value: Aquarius used microwave radiometers to sense how salty the top layer of the ocean is. Salt changes how dense seawater is, so the maps help explain ocean currents, rain and evaporation.

facts.value: It could detect a change of about 0.2 grams of salt in a kilogram of seawater, roughly a pinch of salt in a gallon of water.

craft.name: CALIPSO

craft.name: CloudSat

craft.name: CYGNSS

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

craft.name: DSCOVR

craft.name: Earth Observing-1

craft.name: GOES weather satellite

craft.name: GRACE

facts.value: NASA

craft.name: IBEX

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: October 19, 2008

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026; recheck)

facts.label: Mass

facts.value: IBEX catches fast neutral atoms that fly in from the edge of the heliosphere, and builds all-sky maps from them.

craft.name: NICER / SEXTANT
craft.subtitle: An X-ray telescope on the ISS that tested pulsar navigation
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Station Explorer for X-Ray Timing and Navigation (SEXTANT)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Time X-rays from neutron stars; SEXTANT used pulsars like GPS

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: June 3, 2017 (to the ISS)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Science operations ended November 2026, after a pointing motor failed in June 2025; it will be removed from the ISS (recheck)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 1.2 x 1.6 x 1.1 m (model scale approximate)

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 372 kg

facts.label: About
facts.value: NICER measured neutron star sizes by timing X-rays to about 100 nanoseconds. SEXTANT used the same pulses to work out the station's position.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: In 2017 SEXTANT found the station's position to within about 16 km (10 miles) using pulsars alone, while moving at about 28,000 km/h.

craft.name: SWAS
craft.subtitle: Searched for water and oxygen in star-forming clouds

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.value: Ended 2005

facts.value: about 1.63 m x 1.02 m (body)

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: SWAS looked at cold clouds where stars form and found far less oxygen gas than expected.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was briefly woken in 2005 to watch Deep Impact hit comet Tempel 1.

craft.name: Suzaku
craft.subtitle: A Japanese X-ray observatory with NASA-built mirrors

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: X-ray astronomy of black holes, clusters and hot gas

facts.value: JAXA, with NASA

facts.label: About
facts.value: Suzaku carried five X-ray telescopes with mirrors from NASA Goddard and studied hot gas in galaxy clusters.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Before launch it was called Astro-E2; Suzaku is a red bird from Japanese myth.

craft.name: WIRE
craft.subtitle: An infrared telescope that lost its coolant and found a new job

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Infrared survey of starburst galaxies (planned)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.value: March 5, 1999 (UTC)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Re-entered May 10, 2011

facts.value: spacecraft body under 1 m across (recheck)

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: A cover came off early and the frozen hydrogen coolant boiled away within days. Its star tracker was then used to measure starquakes.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: That rescue science made WIRE an early space asteroseismology mission.

craft.name: Spartan 201
craft.subtitle: A Sun-watcher that the Space Shuttle released and caught again

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Study the solar corona and solar wind from a free-flying shuttle payload

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired after its last flight in 1998 (STS-95)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Spartan was set loose by the shuttle's robot arm, flew on its own for a couple of days, and was then grabbed and brought home.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: On STS-87 in 1997 it tumbled after release, and astronauts caught it by hand on a spacewalk.

craft.name: Ulysses
craft.subtitle: The first craft to fly over the Sun's poles

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Study the Sun and solar wind at all latitudes

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: ESA and NASA

facts.label: About
facts.value: To leave the plane of the planets, Ulysses flew to Jupiter and used its gravity to swing up over the Sun's poles.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It flew through the tails of three comets by chance.

craft.name: Clementine
craft.subtitle: Mapped the whole Moon in 1994

facts.value: US Ballistic Missile Defense Organization and NASA

facts.value: Clementine mapped the Moon in 11 colors and its radar hinted at ice in craters near the south pole.

craft.name: SSL 1300 bus
craft.subtitle: A workhorse satellite body, also used for NASA's Psyche

facts.value: Many in service (as of Nov 2026)

facts.value: Over a hundred satellites have been built on this bus. NASA chose it for the Psyche asteroid mission.

facts.value: In 2015 its builder delivered the 100th satellite built on this design, more than any other communications satellite model in orbit at the time.

craft.name: Roman Space Telescope
craft.subtitle: Hubble-sharp images that each cover 100 times more sky

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Wide-field infrared survey: dark energy, exoplanets and the infrared sky

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Launched August 30, 2026; due to reach L2 in early December 2026; first images to be released December 7, 2026 (recheck)

facts.value: Roman has a 2.4 m mirror like Hubble's, but its camera sees about 100 times more sky in each picture.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It is named for Nancy Grace Roman, NASA's first chief astronomer, often called the mother of Hubble.

craft.name: TDRS
craft.subtitle: The relay satellites that keep the ISS and Hubble in touch
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Tracking and Data Relay Satellites (TDRS) (D)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Relay data between spacecraft in low orbit and the ground

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: first April 4, 1983 (STS-6); latest August 18, 2017

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Fleet operating (as of Nov 2026; recheck)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 17 m across the solar arrays (first generation)

facts.label: About
facts.value: From geostationary orbit, a few TDRS satellites give near-constant contact with the ISS, Hubble and many others.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Before TDRS, astronauts lost contact whenever they flew out of range of a ground station.

craft.name: MAVEN
craft.subtitle: Showed how Mars lost its air to space
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN (MAVEN) (A)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Study the upper atmosphere of Mars and how it escapes

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: November 18, 2013

facts.value: Mission ended June 3, 2026; contact was lost December 6, 2025

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 11.4 m across the solar wings

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 2,454 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: MAVEN showed that the solar wind strips gas from Mars, which helps explain how the planet went from wet to dry.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It also relayed data from the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.

craft.name: Rosetta
craft.subtitle: Orbited a comet and dropped a lander on it

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Orbit and land on comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: ESA, with NASA instruments

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: March 2, 2004

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Ended September 30, 2016, with a controlled landing on the comet

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 2.8 x 2.1 x 2.0 m body; 32 m across the solar arrays

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 3,000 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Rosetta followed the comet for two years as it passed the Sun and released the Philae lander in 2014.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its solar arrays had to work at more than 5 times Earth's distance from the Sun.

craft.name: Gateway
craft.subtitle: A lunar space station NASA designed, then paused in 2026
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Gateway Lunar Space Station

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Lunar-orbit outpost for Artemis crews

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, with ESA, JAXA, CSA, the UAE and industry

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: Never launched

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Paused in its current form by NASA in March 2026; some hardware to be reused (as of Nov 2026; recheck)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: model about 18 x 30 x 39 m

facts.label: About
facts.value: Gateway was designed to orbit the Moon in a long, stretched orbit, giving crews a place to live, work and transfer to lunar landers. In 2026 NASA paused it to focus on a base on the lunar surface.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its power module was designed to use solar electric propulsion, the same kind of Hall thrusters that drive NASA's Psyche spacecraft.

craft.name: ACES suit
craft.subtitle: The orange launch and entry suit of the shuttle era
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Advanced Crew Escape Suit

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A full pressure suit worn during launch and landing

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: Space Shuttle, 1994 to 2011

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: sized to the astronaut; model about 2 m tall

facts.label: About
facts.value: If the cabin lost pressure, the suit kept the crew alive. It also carried a parachute harness, life raft and survival gear for bailing out.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its orange color, nicknamed the pumpkin suit, makes a crew member easy to spot in the ocean.

craft.name: Astronaut

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: NASA outreach model

facts.label: About
facts.value: A person in a suit is the easiest way to judge how big a spacecraft is. Put this next to anything in the fleet in AR.

craft.name: Spacewalk glove
craft.subtitle: The hardest part of a spacesuit to get right

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A pressurized spacewalk glove

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: NASA spacesuits

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 30 cm long (model scale approximate)

facts.label: About
facts.value: A pressurized glove fights every finger movement, so hand fatigue is one of the biggest limits on how long a spacewalk can go.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: NASA ran Centennial Challenges for better astronaut gloves in 2007 and 2009.

craft.name: EMU spacesuit
craft.subtitle: The spacewalk suit used on the shuttle and the ISS

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A self-contained spacewalk suit with its own life support

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: Space Shuttle and International Space Station, since the early 1980s (first spacewalk in 1983)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: model about 2 m tall

facts.label: About
facts.value: The backpack holds oxygen, a cooling water loop and power for spacewalks that often last six to eight hours.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: On a two-person spacewalk, one suit has red stripes on the legs so the two astronauts can be told apart.

craft.name: Gemini spacesuit
craft.subtitle: Worn on America's first spacewalk

facts.value: A pressure suit for Gemini missions

facts.label: Used on

facts.label: Real size

facts.label: About
facts.value: Gemini suits were built for both cabin wear and spacewalks. Ed White wore one for the first American spacewalk in June 1965.

craft.name: Mark III suit
craft.subtitle: A hard-bodied test suit for walking on other worlds

facts.value: NASA test programs

facts.label: Real size

facts.value: The Mark III mixed hard and soft parts so a wearer could bend, kneel and walk more easily than in older suits.

craft.name: Mercury spacesuit
craft.subtitle: The silver suit of America's first astronauts

facts.value: A pressure suit for Mercury flights

facts.value: Project Mercury, 1961 to 1963

facts.label: Real size

facts.label: About
facts.value: It was adapted from a Navy high-altitude jet pilot suit and coated in aluminum for the famous silver look.

craft.name: Z-2 suit

facts.label: Fun fact

craft.name: Spacesuit helmet
craft.subtitle: A clear bubble helmet for spacewalks

facts.value: A spacesuit pressure helmet

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: NASA spacesuits

facts.value: The clear bubble holds pressure; spacewalkers add a visor assembly with lights, cameras and a gold sun visor on top.

craft.name: Robonaut 2

facts.value: R2 was built by NASA and General Motors. It flew to the ISS in 2011 on the last flight of Discovery and later got legs for climbing.

craft.name: Space Exploration Vehicle

facts.value: The cabin could sit on a 12-wheel chassis on the Moon or Mars, or on a sled with thrusters for visiting asteroids. Crews would climb into suits through ports on the back.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: An early version drove across the Arizona desert in NASA's Desert RATS field tests.

craft.name: Habitat Demonstration Unit

facts.value: NASA teams lived and worked in the HDU during desert field tests to learn how a surface habitat should be laid out.

facts.value: RASSOR's two bucket drums spin in opposite directions, so their digging forces cancel. That lets a light robot dig in low gravity without getting pushed away.

craft.name: Canadarm

craft.name: Scarecrow

facts.value: The SLIC carried the Wide Field Camera 3 and new batteries up to Hubble in 2009, using a carbon composite frame to save weight.

craft.name: Crew lock bag

facts.value: Everything on a spacewalk is tethered or bagged, because anything let go drifts off. This bag carries tools and small parts.

facts.label: About
facts.value: The tank fed the three main engines for about eight and a half minutes, then dropped away and broke up over the ocean. It was the only part of the shuttle that was not reused.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: The first two tanks were painted white. NASA stopped painting them to save about 270 kg, which left the orange foam showing.

craft.name: Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster
craft.subtitle: Two of these lifted the shuttle off the pad

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A reusable solid rocket booster

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: Space Shuttle, 1981 to 2011

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 45.5 m long, 3.7 m across

facts.label: About
facts.value: The two boosters gave most of the thrust at liftoff, burned for about two minutes, then parachuted into the ocean to be recovered and refilled.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Upgraded versions with five segments instead of four now fly on the SLS rocket.

craft.name: Orbiter Docking System
craft.subtitle: The shuttle's docking port for Mir and the ISS

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: An airlock and docking mechanism in the shuttle's payload bay

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: Space Shuttle visits to Mir and the ISS, 1995 to 2011

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 4.6 m across the bay (model scale approximate)

facts.label: About
facts.value: The system sat in the front of the payload bay. Its docking ring latched onto the station so crews could float between the two.

craft.name: Crawler-transporter
craft.subtitle: Carries rockets to the launch pad at walking pace

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A tracked vehicle that moves rockets and launch platforms

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: Apollo, Space Shuttle and Artemis, since 1965

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 40 m x 35 m

facts.label: About
facts.value: The crawler drives under a mobile launcher, lifts it with the rocket on top and carries it about 5.5 to 6.8 km to the pad (6.8 km to Pad 39B, where Artemis launches) while keeping it level.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its top speed with a load is about 1.6 km/h (1 mph).

craft.name: Mobile Launcher
craft.subtitle: The launch tower that rides with the SLS rocket

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A launch platform with an umbilical tower

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: Artemis SLS launches

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 116 m tall: a 108 m tower on a 7.6 m high base

facts.label: About
facts.value: The rocket is stacked on the launcher inside the VAB, and the crawler carries both to the pad. Arms on the tower feed propellant, power and air until liftoff.

craft.name: Vehicle Assembly Building
craft.subtitle: Where NASA stacks its biggest rockets

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A rocket assembly building at Kennedy Space Center

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: Apollo, Space Shuttle and Artemis, since 1966

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 160 m tall, 218 m long, 158 m wide

facts.label: About
facts.value: The VAB was built to stack Saturn V rockets standing up. Its high bay doors are the largest in the world.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Each of its four high bay doors is 456 feet (139 m) tall, the largest doors in the world, and takes about 45 minutes to open.

craft.name: DSN 70 m antenna
craft.subtitle: The giant dishes that talk to Voyager

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A 70 m radio antenna of NASA's Deep Space Network

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: Goldstone (California), Madrid (Spain) and Canberra (Australia)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: dish 70 m across

facts.label: About
facts.value: Three sites spaced around the globe keep at least one dish facing every deep space mission as Earth turns.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: The 70 m dish in Canberra is the only antenna that can send commands to Voyager 2.

craft.name: DSN 34 m antenna
craft.subtitle: The workhorse dishes of the Deep Space Network

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A 34 m beam waveguide antenna

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: NASA Deep Space Network, all three sites

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: dish 34 m across

facts.label: About
facts.value: The 34 m dishes handle most deep space traffic and can be linked together to act like a bigger antenna.

craft.name: CubeSat 1U
craft.subtitle: A satellite the size of a coffee mug box

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A one-unit CubeSat

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: Universities, companies and NASA, since 2003

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 10 x 10 x 10 cm body, no more than 2 kg (early rules said 1.33 kg)

facts.label: About
facts.value: CubeSats are built from standard 10 cm cubes, so they can share rides to orbit in spring-loaded dispensers.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: The standard was created in 1999 by Cal Poly and Stanford.

craft.name: CubeSat 2U
craft.subtitle: Two CubeSat units stacked together

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A two-unit CubeSat

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: Universities, companies and NASA

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 10 x 10 x 22.7 cm body

facts.label: About
facts.value: Stacking units gives room for bigger batteries, cameras or experiments while still fitting a standard dispenser.

craft.name: IceCube
craft.subtitle: A CubeSat that mapped cloud ice from space

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Test a submillimeter radiometer for measuring cloud ice

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA Goddard

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: launched April 18, 2017 to the ISS; released May 16, 2017

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Mission complete; re-entered October 3, 2018

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 3U CubeSat, about 10 x 10 x 34 cm

facts.label: About
facts.value: IceCube made the first global map of cloud ice at 883 GHz, a frequency never used from orbit before.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was only planned to work for about a month, but it kept collecting data for more than a year.

craft.name: MiRaTA
craft.subtitle: A CubeSat that tested a tiny weather sounder

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Test microwave sounding of temperature and humidity from a CubeSat

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and MIT Lincoln Laboratory

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: November 18, 2017

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Contact lost in January 2018; re-entered the atmosphere October 23, 2025 (recheck before publish)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 3U CubeSat, about 10 x 10 x 34 cm

facts.label: About
facts.value: MiRaTA tried to do with a shoebox-sized satellite what large weather satellites do with much bigger sounders.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was designed to use GPS signals bending through the atmosphere to check its readings, a new trick for calibrating weather sensors.

craft.name: Constellation-X
craft.subtitle: A planned X-ray observatory that became part of IXO

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A proposed X-ray observatory

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: NASA concept, 1990s to 2008

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 10 m long (model scale approximate)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Constellation-X would have studied black holes and hot gas with large X-ray mirrors. In 2008 it merged with ESA's XEUS into IXO.

craft.name: IXO
craft.subtitle: A proposed X-ray observatory with a 20 m extendable bench

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A proposed X-ray observatory

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: NASA, ESA and JAXA concept, 2008 to 2011

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 23 m long with the bench extended

facts.label: About
facts.value: IXO planned a mirror more than 3 m across and an optical bench that would extend to a 20 m focal length in space. The project was cancelled; ESA's Athena grew from it.

craft.name: ATLAST
craft.subtitle: A concept for a giant ultraviolet and optical telescope
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Advanced Technology Large-Aperture Space Telescope (ATLAST)

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A proposed large space telescope

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: NASA concept studies, 2000s to 2010s

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: model about 27 m long

facts.label: About
facts.value: ATLAST studies looked at mirrors 8 to 16 m across to search for signs of life on planets around other stars. The idea fed into LUVOIR and now the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

craft.name: LISA
craft.subtitle: Three spacecraft that will listen for gravitational waves
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) (2006)

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: One spacecraft of a planned gravitational wave observatory

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: ESA mission with NASA, planned for the 2030s (2006 NASA design shown)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: each about 2.6 m across

facts.label: About
facts.value: Three LISA spacecraft will fly in a triangle 2.5 million km on a side and measure tiny changes in distance with lasers as gravitational waves pass.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: ESA adopted LISA as a mission in 2024.

craft.name: DESDynI
craft.subtitle: A radar concept that became NISAR
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Deformation, Ecosystem Structure, and Dynamics of Ice (DESDynI)

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A proposed radar and lidar Earth mission

facts.label: Used on
facts.value: NASA concept, 2007 to 2010s

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: model about 21 m across

facts.label: About
facts.value: DESDynI was planned to measure ground movement from earthquakes, ice sheet changes and forest structure. Its radar part became NISAR, built with India.

craft.name: DART
craft.subtitle: Crashed into an asteroid on purpose, and moved it
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Test planetary defense by hitting an asteroid moon

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (APL)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: November 23, 2021 (10:21 p.m. Pacific), from California

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Impacted Dimorphos on September 26, 2022 (mission complete)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: main body about 1.1 x 1.2 x 1.3 m (about 1.8 x 1.9 x 2.6 m with thrusters and equipment); about 18 to 19 m across the solar arrays

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 610 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: DART hit the small moonlet Dimorphos at about 6 km/s and shortened its orbit around Didymos by about 32 minutes.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It steered itself for the final hours using its camera, DRACO.

craft.name: Orion
craft.subtitle: NASA's capsule for Artemis crews

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Carry astronauts to the Moon and back

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, with ESA's service module

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: first flight December 5, 2014 (EFT-1); Artemis I November 16, 2022; Artemis II, the first crewed flight, April 1, 2026

facts.label: Status
facts.value: In service. Artemis II carried four astronauts around the Moon, April 1 to 10, 2026 (as of Nov 2026; recheck for Artemis III)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: crew module 5.0 m across

facts.label: About
facts.value: Orion's crew module holds four astronauts. Its heat shield is the largest of its kind, built to survive coming home from the Moon at about 40,000 km/h.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: On Artemis I in 2022, Orion flew farther from Earth than any spacecraft built for humans had before.
